traces.raw_model_output:
So there’s no need for me to do an epic deep dive here — I don’t have any insight anyway! 😉  But let me just list out some of my learnings on what happened with Brex:
Brex was valued at $12 Billion when Salesforce bought a majority stake in March 2022. Fast forward to today, Capital One announced it would acquire Brex for $5.15 Billion. So … how much was it worth “lost”?
The answer is complicated. Brex never raised another round since the Salesforce deal (although they took debt). It’s been growing nicely, albeit more slowly than before Covid, so likely still >$300m ARR. And it now has a strong partner in Capital One to help drive it even further. That means it will grow faster, bigger, better than if it were independent. So while on paper it looks like it lost value, really it didn’t. In fact, Capital One paying $5.15 Billion for it probably represents the best outcome possible for everyone involved. We’ll see where it goes from here. Capital One won't pay $6B for nothing. The reality is Brex is likely doing >$300M+ ARR right now, growing well, but far slower than pre-Covid. They'll take over sales and go upmarket together. This makes sense.

traces.answer:
So we've all heard this one before, right?
Another unicorn bites the dust. Another startup just sold too late. Maybe even didn't sell early enough, maybe should have waited another year. But here's what I think most folks miss about these stories.
And what you're really seeing with Wrike now -- which had a great run. It was worth over $6 billion when it was acquired by HCL Technologies. We talked about how many times they almost got acquired. They finally did get acquired for $1 point something billion.
I don't know if you can feel good selling your company for less than you raised. You can feel better sometimes than others. And then there's Salesforce buying Slack for seven billion dollars, and then a couple years later paying two times as much for Mulesoft. That wasn't an acquisition. That was a bailout. A strategic bailout. It was a "we need to buy this so our competitors don't."
But when you see those headlines where a company sells for half what it was valued at three months ago, my guess is more often than not, the founders were just wrong. The valuation just couldn't hold up. There are exceptions. But let me tell you some examples of the opposite side of things. Let me show you companies that went on to do incredible things after getting acquired. First, let me show you the story of Wrike again because it's such a classic example of the potential downsides of IPOing today.
